passage:
I sat in the Monday review, so I can tell you exactly what happened, but not why.
On Thursday, Bhavesh, our newest analyst, had shown three of us a way to cut the monthly report from two days to two hours. Sharmila was one of the three. She said, "Nice."
On Monday, in front of the regional head, Sharmila put up the same flowchart with small colour changes and said, "I've been thinking about how we could speed up reporting." She didn't say Bhavesh's name once.
Bhavesh stared at his notebook.
Now, what I know about Sharmila: there have been layoff rumours for months, and she was passed over for promotion in March. At lunch she once said, "We're a team, credit is shared anyway." I think she might be scared. I don't know if that's the whole story.
What I do know is Bhavesh hasn't shared an idea in a meeting since.
Nazia

qa.q: How long did Bhavesh's idea cut the monthly report down to?
qa.a: It cut the monthly report from two days to two hours.

qa.q: What does Nazia suspect might be driving Sharmila, and how sure is Nazia?
qa.a: Nazia suspects fear, given the layoff rumours and the missed promotion, but openly says that may not be the whole story.

qa.q: What could someone in the Monday review have done at the key moment?
qa.a: Nazia or another person who saw Thursday's demo could have said calmly that the flowchart was Bhavesh's work, so his name was on it.

qa.q: How has Sharmila's choice affected Bhavesh?
qa.a: Bhavesh stared at his notebook and has not shared an idea in a meeting since, so the credit-taking has silenced a new analyst.

grounding: Nazia watches Sharmila present a junior's idea as her own, possibly driven by fear of layoffs, and telling herself credit is shared anyway.

passage:
Day one. Minakshi, two months into the team, posted in the project chat: "What if we sent reminders by voice call for older customers?" Tushar read it on the metro and thought, that's good. That's really good. Then: why didn't I think of it?
Day three. The client call. The director asked for fresh ideas. Tushar's mouth was dry. Two seniors had been let go last quarter. He heard himself say, "I was thinking we could try voice-call reminders for older customers." The director nodded. "Great, Tushar, lead that."
Minakshi said nothing. On the way out Tushar told himself, it's a team, ideas belong to the team.
Day ten. Minakshi hadn't posted in the chat since. Tushar noticed. Every time he opened the project folder, his stomach turned slightly, like he'd borrowed something and hadn't returned it.

qa.q: What did the director say after Tushar spoke on the call?
qa.a: The director said, "Great, Tushar, lead that."

qa.q: What was Tushar afraid of when he spoke on the client call?
qa.a: Tushar was afraid of being let go like the two seniors and wanted recognition, so fear pushed him to present Minakshi's idea as his own.

qa.q: At which moment could Tushar still have put things right?
qa.a: On the call, or on Day ten when he noticed the silence, Tushar could have said the idea was Minakshi's and handed Minakshi the lead.

qa.q: How has Minakshi been affected by what happened on the call?
qa.a: Minakshi has stopped posting in the chat, which suggests Minakshi no longer feels safe sharing ideas with the team.

grounding: Driven by fear of job loss, Tushar presents a junior's idea as his own and tells himself ideas belong to the team, while his unease grows.

passage:
The VP's review got moved to 9 am with ten minutes' notice, and Ojas had only one good slide: Swati's. Her idea to bundle the late deliveries by pin code had saved the team hours last month.
Walking to the conference room, he rehearsed. There were rumours of restructuring. Two leads had already been let go. If he walked in with nothing of his own, he'd be next.
"We came up with a new routing approach," he told the VP. "I've been pushing it for a while."
The VP nodded, impressed. "Good thinking, Ojas."
He felt a warm rush, then a small cold drop in his stomach. It's a team idea anyway, he told himself. We all share credit. That's what teams do.
Back at his desk, Swati looked up. "How did it go?"
"Fine," he said, not meeting her eyes. He opened an email to the VP about Swati's part, then closed it. Later, he thought. Tomorrow.

qa.q: What was Swati's idea?
qa.a: Her idea to bundle the late deliveries by pin code.

qa.q: What was Ojas feeling as he walked into the review and after the praise?
qa.a: Ojas was afraid of being let go in the restructuring, and then felt a rush of pride at the VP's praise followed by a cold drop of guilt.

qa.q: What could Ojas still do to set it right?
qa.a: Send the email he opened, naming Swati's part to the VP today, instead of putting it off until tomorrow.

qa.q: What might Swati feel if she learned what Ojas said in the meeting?
qa.a: Swati would likely feel betrayed and unseen, since her idea saved the team hours and all she heard was 'Fine'.

grounding: Shows a team lead presenting a colleague's idea as his own out of fear of being let go, telling himself the team shares credit anyway.

passage:
In the Mumbai co-working space, the founder called Zubin over after the demo. "That pricing insight was brilliant. Where did it come from?"
It had come from Zeenat's spreadsheet, the one she had stayed late three nights to build. Zubin had only made the slides prettier.
"Oh, I was playing around with the numbers," he said, and the founder slapped his shoulder. "This is why you're going places."
Zubin had waited two years to hear a sentence like that. At home nobody had ever said it. He felt ten feet tall.
In the lift he told himself: we're a small team, everything is shared, Zeenat doesn't care about credit. She isn't even on social media.
When the founder posted on the company page, "Shout-out to Zubin for our new pricing model!", Zeenat liked it. An hour later, she unliked it. Zubin saw the notification and put his phone face down.

qa.q: How many nights had Zeenat stayed late to build the spreadsheet?
qa.a: Zeenat had stayed late three nights.

qa.q: Why did Zubin claim the pricing insight?
qa.a: Zubin felt proud and hungry for recognition, having waited two years for praise like that, and felt ten feet tall hearing it.

qa.q: What could Zubin do after seeing the unlike?
qa.a: Tell the founder and the team that the pricing model came from Zeenat's spreadsheet, and ask for the post to name her.

qa.q: What might Zeenat's like and then unlike suggest?
qa.a: Zeenat may have first tried to be gracious, then felt hurt and angry as it sank in that her work had been posted under Zubin's name.

grounding: Shows a young employee claiming a colleague's insight out of hunger for recognition and telling himself credit in a small team is shared.

passage:
"Vaibhav, the client deck. Slide six. That's my campaign idea."
"It's the team's idea, Uma. We all brainstormed."
"I pitched it to you alone, on Monday, in the pantry. You said 'interesting' and changed the subject."
"And then I developed it."
"You changed the font."
Vaibhav rubbed his forehead. "Look. Do you know how many new managers they hired this quarter? Three. All younger than me. If I walk into that client meeting with nothing, I'm gone."
"So you took mine."
"I told myself it doesn't matter whose name is on it. Credit gets shared eventually."
"Does it? My name isn't anywhere."
Silence.
"Okay," he said finally. "I'll add you to the presenters for Thursday. And I'll tell the director it was yours."
"Today?"
He nodded. "Today."

qa.q: Where did Uma first pitch the campaign idea to Vaibhav?
qa.a: In the pantry, on Monday, to him alone.

qa.q: What was Vaibhav afraid of when he took the idea?
qa.a: Vaibhav was afraid of being replaced, since three younger managers had been hired that quarter.

qa.q: What did Uma do that made Vaibhav act?
qa.a: Uma stated the facts calmly, where and when she pitched it, and pressed for a clear step today, not a vague promise.

qa.q: How does Uma see Vaibhav's 'credit gets shared eventually'?
qa.a: Uma sees it as an excuse, since her name wasn't anywhere, and she won't let silence stand.

grounding: Shows a manager who took a junior's idea out of fear of being replaced, justifying it as shared credit until he is challenged.

passage: I've told this story to exactly one person, so here goes. Last spring at the agency, Simran, our newest designer, sketched an idea for the bakery chain's campaign on a napkin at lunch: bread rising like a sunrise. It was brilliant. Two days later I presented it to the client as something I had been developing. I didn't mention her. In my head I had reasons. I was the team lead; my name was on the account; credit belongs to the whole team anyway, right? And there was the part I didn't say even to myself: our boss had been praising Simran all month, and I was scared that in a year she'd have my job. The client loved it. I felt sick in the car. When Simran saw the deck, she didn't say anything. She just stopped sharing ideas at lunch. That silence cost the team more than any campaign earned. In June I finally told our boss the idea was Simran's, and I told Simran too. I'm Vandana, and I'm still embarrassed.

qa.q: What was Simran's idea for the campaign?
qa.a: Bread rising like a sunrise.

qa.q: What was Vandana afraid of when taking the credit?
qa.a: Vandana felt scared that Simran, praised by the boss all month, would take Vandana's job within a year.

qa.q: What repair did Vandana make, and what else could help?
qa.a: Vandana told the boss and Simran the truth; naming Simran on the work and inviting her ideas again could rebuild trust.

qa.q: How did Simran respond to seeing the deck?
qa.a: Simran said nothing but stopped sharing ideas at lunch, suggesting she felt hurt and no longer safe offering her work.

grounding: Shows a team lead presenting a junior's idea as their own out of fear of being replaced, telling themselves the team shares credit anyway.
